etymology: From Old French cale, a close-fitting cap; rendering Hebrew shebīsīm, the netted or checkered headdresses of the daughters of Zion, first named in the inventory of Isaiah 3.
biblical_def: Cauls are the netted caps or woven head-tires that open the LORD’s inventory of Zion’s finery: “In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon” (Isa 3:18). The judgment falls not on cloth and wire but on what the wardrobe had come to mean, for the charge is read out first: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes” (Isa 3:16). Then follows the strangest list in the prophets — twenty-one articles of dress named one by one, as an officer inventories the goods of a house under seizure. The LORD counts the finery because the wearers counted it; He names each piece because each piece had become a name for the self. The caul crowned the head, and the head was the seat of the haughtiness. Let the reader mark that Scripture is not against ornament — the LORD Himself decks His bride (Eze 16:11-13) — but against glory worn as armor of pride. Where adornment becomes identity, God writes an inventory; and the day comes when “instead of well set hair” there is baldness (Isa 3:24). The covering that never falls is another kind: the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4).
webster_summary: The netted headdresses opening Isaiah’s inventory of Zion’s finery — adornment become identity, counted for seizure.

scriptures: In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:

And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: The caul heads Scripture’s case against the cult of adornment — the age that makes appearance an identity is older than it thinks, and already inventoried.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not the cap but the cult. Isaiah’s Jerusalem had made the wardrobe a self — haughtiness dressed, catalogued, and paraded — and the present age has industrialized the same religion: the curated image, the filtered face, appearance as the soul’s résumé. And the men of the age are not behind the daughters in it.

The recovered principle is the inventory itself. God names every article the heart leans on, and He can take away the whole list in a day; the only adorning He prices is the one He cannot seize — the hidden man of the heart, a meek and quiet spirit, in the sight of God of great price (1Pe 3:4). Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised (Pro 31:30).

etymology: “Tire” from attire, a head-ornament; rendering Hebrew saharōnīm, crescent-shaped pendants — “round tires like the moon” — worn by Zion’s daughters and hung on Midianite camels.
biblical_def: The round tires like the moon are crescent ornaments — little moons of gold hung at the neck or brow, named among the finery the Lord will take away (Isa 3:18). The same Hebrew word appears in the days of Gideon: when he overthrew the kings of Midian he “took away the ornaments that were on their camels’ necks” (Jdg 8:21), crescents hung even on beasts, the jewelry of a moon-venerating desert people (Jdg 8:26). That pedigree is the sting of the phrase. The daughters of Zion, covenant children of the God who made the moon, were wearing the moon — the fashionable amulet-shapes of the nations around them, badges borrowed from another devotion. Fashion is rarely neutral for long; the trinkets of a culture carry the theology of a culture, and Jerusalem’s jewelry box had quietly filled with Midian. The LORD’s answer is not a lecture on astronomy but an inventory of seizure: the little moons will set in a day. Let the believer read his own ornaments — and emblems, and slogans worn on the body — with open eyes: what a man hangs about his neck tells whose he is. The saints wear a better sign, not shaped like the moon but sealed by the Spirit (Eph 1:13), and their beauty waxes when every borrowed crescent has waned.
webster_summary: Crescent pendants — “round tires like the moon” — pagan-pedigreed fashion on covenant daughters; the trinkets of a culture carry its theology.
webster_full: ROUND TIRES, crescent-shaped ornaments of gold, worn at the neck or brow.

What a man hangs about his neck tells whose he is.

In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,
corruption_summary: The crescents expose fashion as a carrier of devotion: Jerusalem’s jewelry box had quietly filled with Midian, and the age’s emblems still preach whose the wearer is.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is borrowed devotion worn as style. The covenant daughters were not praying to the moon; they were merely wearing it — which is how another theology always arrives, as an accessory before it is an altar. The present age sells its own crescents: emblems, brands, and slogans hung on the body whose creeds the wearer would blush to recite.

The recovered principle is discernment at the jewelry box. The trinkets of a culture carry the theology of a culture, and the LORD inventories what His people wear allegiance to. The believer’s badge is not a shape of gold but the seal of the Spirit (Eph 1:13); let nothing hang about the neck that another god could claim as his sign.

etymology: From Old French moufle, a covering; rendering Hebrew re‘ālōth, the fluttering, spangled half-veils of the daughters of Zion (Isa 3:19).
biblical_def: Mufflers are the light, trembling veils — spangled half-coverings that fluttered before the face — named in the second line of the inventory: “The chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers” (Isa 3:19). The Hebrew suggests a shimmering, quivering thing, a veil worn not to hide the face but to advertise it — concealment turned coquetry. Here the inventory touches something subtler than gold: the fashion that plays at modesty. A true covering says, this beauty is kept for its covenant place; the muffler of Zion’s daughters said, guess. It belonged to the same walk as the “wanton eyes” and the mincing steps (Isa 3:16) — a wardrobe of suggestion, veiling as performance. The LORD is not mocked by fabric: He reads the message of a garment as surely as the message of a tongue, and He listed the mufflers with the rest of the bravery to be taken away in a day. Let the believer learn that modesty is a matter of intent before it is a matter of inches. Rebekah took a vail to meet her bridegroom in honest reverence (Gen 24:65); Zion’s daughters took a shimmer to the street. The garment may be cousin; the hearts are strangers. God weighs what the clothing is saying, and to whom.
webster_summary: The spangled, fluttering half-veils of Zion’s daughters — concealment turned coquetry; God reads the message of a garment.

corruption_summary: The muffler names the oldest fashion trick — modesty worn as suggestion; the age has made veiling-as-performance an entire industry.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is performance dressed as propriety. The muffler kept the letter of the veil and inverted its spirit — covering as a lure — and the present age has built industries on the same inversion: the calculated tease marketed as empowerment, garments engineered to say guess while claiming to say no.

The recovered principle is intent before inches. Modesty is not a hemline arithmetic but a heart’s message: Rebekah’s vail honored a bridegroom; the muffler advertised a wearer. Women professing godliness adorn themselves with shamefacedness and sobriety (1Ti 2:9) — and men of God keep their own wardrobe of suggestion under the same law, for the LORD reads what clothing says, and to whom.

etymology: From Old French bonet, a cap; rendering Hebrew pe’ērīm, an ornamental headdress — worn by Aaron’s sons “for glory and for beauty,” and by Zion’s daughters for vanity.
biblical_def: The bonnet leads the third line of Isaiah’s inventory: “The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings” (Isa 3:20). But this headdress has a double life in Scripture, and the doubleness is the doctrine. The very same adornment was commanded for the priests: “for Aaron’s sons thou shalt make coats… and bonnets shalt thou make for them, for glory and for beauty” (Exo 28:40); and the bridegroom of Isaiah 61 “decketh himself with ornaments” — the same Hebrew word, a pe’ēr (Isa 61:10). One word, two heads: on the servant of the sanctuary it is glory; on the haughty street it is plunder for the seizure-list. Ornament, then, is not the sin; unconsecrated ornament is. Glory God assigns to an office He delights in; glory the self assigns to the self He inventories. The gospel does not end the bonnet but restores it: to them that mourn in Zion the LORD promises “beauty for ashes” — literally a pe’ēr for ashes (Isa 61:3), the festal headdress set on repentant heads by God’s own hand. Let the believer wear nothing he has crowned himself with; the only glory that survives the inventory is the glory God Himself sets on.
webster_summary: One headdress, two heads: commanded on priests “for glory and for beauty,” inventoried on the haughty — glory is safe only where God assigns it.

And for Aaron's sons thou shalt make coats, and thou shalt make for them girdles, and bonnets shalt thou make for them, for glory and for beauty.

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: The bonnet splits the age’s confusion about glory: adornment God assigns is holy; adornment the self assigns to the self goes on the seizure-list.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is self-coronation. The same headdress that was holy on a priest was plunder on the proud, and the difference was never the fabric but the assigning hand. The present age knows only self-assigned glory — self-styled, self-titled, self-crowned — and cannot imagine beauty as something conferred rather than claimed.

The recovered principle is glory by assignment. God delights to beautify: He commanded bonnets for glory and for beauty, and He promises the festal pe’er for ashes to them that mourn. The believer refuses every crown of his own weaving and receives what God sets on — for the only ornament that survives the inventory is the one His hand bestowed.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew pe’erim, bonnets crown both the consecrated priest and the haughty daughter — the assigning hand, not the fabric, decides which.

etymology: In Isaiah’s inventory, rendering Hebrew bāttē hannephesh — literally “houses of the soul” — the little perfume-boxes hung about the neck of the daughters of Zion.
biblical_def: The tablets of Isaiah 3:20 are not writing-slates but scent-boxes — small ornamental cases of perfume worn at the neck. The Hebrew name is the arresting thing: bāttē hannephesh, “houses of the soul,” for the nephesh is the breath, the life, the soul itself, and the perfumed breath of the box was its little indwelling spirit. There is the whole spiritual biography of Isaiah’s Jerusalem in one item of jewelry: souls so shrunken that they could be housed in an amulet; life reduced to fragrance, identity to an accessory, the nephesh to a nice smell. The LORD lists the soul-houses with the rest of the bravery to be taken away, and the sentence that closes the inventory answers them exactly: “instead of sweet smell there shall be stink” (Isa 3:24) — the day the little houses are seized, the tenant is exposed. Let the believer ask where his own soul is housed. The age still sells houses of the soul — wardrobes, feeds, follower-counts, bottles — small containers for a thing made to dwell in God. “Thou hast made us for Thyself”; the soul’s true house is not hung about the neck: “he that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psa 91:1).
webster_summary: The perfume-boxes of Isaiah 3 — in Hebrew “houses of the soul”; souls shrunken small enough to live in an amulet.

corruption_summary: “Houses of the soul” the size of a locket: the age still miniaturizes the nephesh into accessories, feeds, and fragrances — and the tenant is exposed when they’re seized.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the miniaturized soul. Isaiah’s Jerusalem housed the nephesh in a scent-box; the present age houses it in a wardrobe, a feed, a follower-count, a brand — containers small enough to purchase, which is precisely their appeal. A soul that fits its accessories has already lost the argument of Matthew 16:26.

The recovered principle is the soul’s true dwelling. The nephesh was made to be housed in God — dwelling in the secret place of the most High, hidden with Christ (Col 3:3) — and every lesser house will be seized on the day the sweet smell turns. The believer keeps his soul where no inventory reaches.

etymology: Rendering Hebrew nezāmīm and kindred words; rings of gold for ear or nose — bridal gift, buried idol-token, raw material of the golden calf, and item of Zion’s inventoried finery.
biblical_def: No ornament in Scripture has a stranger résumé than the earring. It is a bridal honor: Abraham’s servant adorned Rebekah with a golden earring at the well (Gen 24:22). It is an idol’s token: when Jacob purged his house of strange gods, the household surrendered “all their earrings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak” (Gen 35:4) — buried with the idols they served. It is the raw material of apostasy: “all the people brake off the golden earrings which were in their ears, and brought them unto Aaron” (Exo 32:3), and the calf came out of that gold. And it is a line in Isaiah’s inventory of haughtiness (Isa 3:20). One ring, four masters — covenant love, buried superstition, molten idolatry, paraded pride. The metal never changed; the heart behind it did every time. Herein is the Bible’s whole theology of things: gold is not good or evil, but it is never idle — it flows toward what the heart worships, and an earring can end on a bride or in a calf within a single generation. Let the believer ask of every possession not “is it lawful?” only, but “which master is this serving, and what could it be melted into tomorrow?”
webster_summary: One ring, four masters: Rebekah’s bridal gold, Jacob’s buried idol-tokens, the calf’s raw material, Zion’s paraded pride — gold flows toward what the heart worships.

scriptures: And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which were in their hand, and all their earrings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem.

And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold;
corruption_summary: The earring’s résumé refutes the age’s two errors about things — that possessions are innocent, and that possessions are evil; gold is never idle, it serves the reigning heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the pretended neutrality of wealth and adornment. The age insists its gold is “just gold” — mere style, mere savings — while the same metal funds its idols and gilds its pride. Scripture’s earring gives the lie: the identical ring graced a bride, was buried with strange gods, and re-emerged as a calf, according to nothing but the heart in charge of it.

The recovered principle is stewardship as worship. Gold flows toward what the heart adores; therefore the question over every possession is which master it is presently serving. The same ears that gave gold to the calf could have given it to the tabernacle — and later Israel did exactly that, a willing-hearted offering of bracelets and earrings unto the LORD (Exo 35:22). Consecration, not confiscation, is God’s answer to the earring.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew nezamim, earrings pass through bridal love, buried superstition, molten apostasy, and paraded pride — gold serving whatever heart commands it.

etymology: Rendering Hebrew nizmē hā’aph, “rings of the nose”; the nose-ring given to Rebekah as a bridal pledge and inventoried on the daughters of Zion.
biblical_def: The nose jewels close Isaiah’s third line of finery: “The rings, and nose jewels” (Isa 3:21). And like the earring, this ornament has an honorable twin. When Abraham’s servant found Rebekah at the well, “I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands” (Gen 24:47) — the word is the nose-ring, set on her face as the pledge of a bridegroom she had not yet seen. The LORD Himself takes up the image for His covenant with Jerusalem: “And I put a jewel on thy forehead, and earrings in thine ears, and a beautiful crown upon thine head” (Eze 16:12) — He decked her; the ornament was His love-token. That is what makes Isaiah 3 so heavy. The daughters wearing nose jewels in the inventory are wearing the very shape of bridal belonging — but self-bestowed, paraded for the street, tokens of no one’s pledge but their own vanity. An engagement ring with no bridegroom behind it is not romance but costume. Let the believer wear only what love has actually given. The ornaments that survive the day of seizure are the bestowed ones — grace tokens from the Bridegroom’s own hand — and the Church’s jewels are exactly that: “as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels” (Isa 61:10), every one of them His gift.
webster_summary: The bridal nose-ring — Rebekah’s pledge and the LORD’s own love-token in Ezekiel — worn self-bestowed in Isaiah’s inventory: costume without a covenant.

An engagement ring with no bridegroom behind it is costume, not covenant.
scriptures: And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter art thou? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands.
And I put a jewel on thy forehead, and earrings in thine ears, and a beautiful crown upon thine head.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: Bridal tokens worn without a bridegroom: the age dresses in the shapes of covenant belonging — self-bestowed — and calls the costume freedom.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is covenant-shaped costume. The nose jewel meant a pledge received; Zion’s daughters wore the shape of belonging while belonging to no one but themselves. The age repeats it at scale — the language and dress of devotion kept, the Bridegroom dismissed, intimacy’s tokens worn as trophies of autonomy.

The recovered principle is bestowed adornment. Ezekiel’s LORD decks His bride with His own hand, and Isaiah’s bride rejoices in jewels that are entirely gift. The believer wears only what love has actually given — grace-tokens, not self-purchased props — and such ornaments are the only ones the day of seizure cannot touch.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew “rings of the nose,” nose jewels are bridal pledges — honorable when bestowed, inventoried when self-worn without a bridegroom.

etymology: From Old English wimpel, a cloth wound about head and neck; rendering Hebrew mitpāchōth, the ample mantles or shawls of Isaiah 3 — the same garment in which Ruth carried Boaz’s barley.
biblical_def: Wimples are the wide over-mantles of the inventory’s fourth line: “The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins” (Isa 3:22). The Hebrew mitpachath appears exactly once more, and the contrast preaches by itself. On the threshingfloor Boaz said to Ruth, “Bring the vail that thou hast upon thee, and hold it… and he measured six measures of barley, and laid it on her” (Ruth 3:15) — the identical garment, spread out at dawn to carry grain home to a hungry mother-in-law. One wimple hauled barley; the others hung in Jerusalem as bravery for the seizure-list. There is the whole difference between a garment used and a garment worshipped: Ruth’s shawl was a tool of hesed — loyal love in coarse cloth, dusty with provision — while Zion’s wimples were exhibits, spotless because they served no one. The LORD’s inventory does not fall on wool but on waste: on strength dressed up that ought to have been spent. Let the believer put his best fabric to work. The garment that ends dusty with someone else’s barley outlives the one that ends folded in the list of the confiscated; and the virtuous woman’s clothing is “strength and honour” (Pro 31:25) precisely because her hands are full.
webster_summary: The ample mantle of Isaiah’s inventory — the same garment Ruth spread to carry barley: cloth worshipped versus cloth put to work.
webster_full: WIMPLES, wide over-mantles or shawls wound about head and shoulders.
Named in the fourth line of Zion’s inventory (Isa 3:22).
The same Hebrew garment carried Boaz’s six measures of barley for Ruth (Ruth 3:15).
One wimple hauled grain; the others hung as exhibits for the seizure-list.
The inventory falls not on wool but on waste.
scriptures: The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins,
Also he said, Bring the vail that thou hast upon thee, and hold it; and when he had holden it, he measured six measures of barley, and laid it on her: and she went into the city.
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
corruption_summary: The wimple splits wardrobe from worship of wardrobe: Ruth’s shawl carried barley, Zion’s hung spotless because they served no one.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the garment as exhibit. Zion’s wimples were flawless because they were useless — kept for display in a city where widows went unfed. The age has entire closets, feeds, and industries of the same spotlessness: apparel as gallery, never as tool.

The recovered principle is Ruth’s dawn shawl: the believer’s best fabric put to work in loyal love, dusty with someone else’s provision. Women professing godliness adorn themselves “with good works” (1Ti 2:10), and strength and honour are clothing precisely where the hands are full. The garment that serves outlives the garment that poses.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew mitpachoth, wimples are the wide mantles of Isaiah’s inventory — and of Ruth’s barley-carrying, the same cloth in two theologies.

etymology: “Crisping” = curling; rendering Hebrew charītīm, properly bags or purses — the same word for the two bags of silver Gehazi carried; in Isaiah’s inventory, ornamental money-purses (or, as the translators took it, hair-curling irons).
biblical_def: The crisping pins close the fourth line of the inventory (Isa 3:22). The King James translators heard curling-irons for the hair; the Hebrew charītīm is elsewhere unmistakably a money-bag: when Gehazi ran his greedy errand after Naaman, the Syrian “bound two talents of silver in two bags” (2Ki 5:23) — the same word. Either reading lands in the same court, and together they say it best: the vanity purse and the vanity curl are one article of confiscation. Coin and coiffure sit side by side in the seizure-list because they sit side by side in the heart — the twin instruments by which the self is dressed and funded. And the word’s only other appearance is a standing sermon: the charit last seen in Scripture was carrying leprosy home with the silver, for Gehazi took the bags and took Naaman’s plague with them (2Ki 5:27). What the vain purse gathers, it gathers with interest of judgment. Let the believer hold both charitim loosely — the purse and the mirror-drawer alike. “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth” (Mat 6:19); the bags that cannot be seized are the ones Christ commends, “bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not” (Luk 12:33).
webster_summary: Isaiah’s charitim — curling-irons to the translators, money-bags in Kings: coin and coiffure, the twin funds of vanity, confiscated together.

And Naaman said, Be content, take two talents. And he urged him, and bound two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of garments, and laid them upon two of his servants; and they bare them before him.
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
corruption_summary: Coin and coiffure share one Hebrew word and one seizure-list: the purse and the mirror fund the same self, and Gehazi’s bags carried judgment home with the silver.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the funded self. Whether charitim meant curls or coin, Isaiah’s Jerusalem kept both in service of the same idol, and the age does likewise — the beauty industry and the portfolio as the twin ministries of self-worship, each promising what only God bestows.

The recovered principle is treasure relocated. Gehazi’s bags preach what vanity’s purse always carries home; Christ’s counter-offer is bags which wax not old, treasure in the heavens that faileth not (Luk 12:33). The believer holds purse and mirror-drawer loosely, and banks where no inventory, moth, or leprosy reaches.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew charitim — curling-irons or money-bags — the crisping pins close Isaiah’s fourth line: vanity’s coin and coiffure confiscated together.

etymology: From Middle English, an ornamental panel worn over chest and stomach; rendering Hebrew pethīgīl, a rich festal robe — the last article of Zion’s finery, exchanged in judgment for sackcloth.
biblical_def: The stomacher is the last garment named in the inventory, and it appears only in the sentence of exchange that closes it: “And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty” (Isa 3:24). Five exchanges, each a fashion undressed to its opposite: perfume to stench, sash to rope, coiffure to shaved scalp, festal robe to mourning cloth, beauty to branding. The stomacher was the showpiece — the rich panel worn over the breast, the glory-garment of a feast day — and the LORD trades it straight across for sackcloth, the fabric of grief. This is the inventory’s terrible arithmetic: everything the heart had banked in appearance converts, at judgment’s exchange-rate, into its own mockery. Yet Scripture does not leave the exchange running only one way. The same prophet announces the reversal for the penitent: “beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness” (Isa 61:3). The LORD who strips stomacher to sackcloth also clothes sackcloth with gladness: “thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness” (Psa 30:11). Let the believer choose which exchange he stands in — pride’s wardrobe converted downward, or mourning converted up, by grace, into the garments of salvation.
webster_summary: The festal breast-robe closing Zion’s inventory, traded for sackcloth — judgment’s exchange-rate on appearance, and grace’s counter-exchange for the penitent.
webster_full: STOMACHER, a rich ornamental panel or robe worn over the breast; Hebrew pethīgīl.

Grace runs the exchange upward: beauty for ashes, gladness for sackcloth.
scriptures: And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty.

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
corruption_summary: Judgment’s exchange-rate on appearance: the showpiece robe converts to sackcloth — while grace runs the counter-exchange, beauty for ashes, for the penitent.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is banking the self in appearance. Zion’s daughters held their worth in fabric and fragrance, and Isaiah publishes the conversion table for that currency: stink for sweetness, sackcloth for the stomacher, burning instead of beauty. Every culture of image-worship carries the same fine print, and the present one most of all.

The recovered principle is the double exchange. The proud wardrobe converts downward at judgment; but the mourner’s sackcloth converts upward by grace — beauty for ashes, the garment of praise for heaviness, gladness girded on by God’s own hand. Be clothed with humility (1Pe 5:5): it is the one garment judgment cannot strip and the fabric grace loves to gild.
